title: Model food's path and explain absorption

prompts: Without the worked example, explain: Arrange the main stages of the digestive tract and distinguish that path from organs supplying digestive juices.
Without the worked example, explain: Explain absorption as digested nutrients crossing the small-intestine wall, using a counted paper model.

pedagogy.rationale: Record an initial model, build and revise a route, track tokens crossing a model wall, then independently explain a new model and correct a community poster.

prerequisiteAssumptions: Count and subtract whole numbers to twenty, follow an ordered route and explain a simple model orally or in writing.

misconceptions.description: The swallowed food route is drawn through the liver or pancreas instead of distinguishing the juices they supply.
misconceptions.response: Keep the continuous food route separate from the liver and pancreas, which supply digestive juices.

misconceptions.description: The stomach is treated as the place where all nutrients enter the body.
misconceptions.response: Most digested nutrients are absorbed through the small-intestine wall.

misconceptions.description: Nutrients that cross the wall are treated as disappearing from the model total.
misconceptions.response: Keep transferred tokens visible in the body region. Count both regions to conserve the total.

misconceptions.description: The starting count is reported as still inside after tokens have crossed the wall.
misconceptions.response: The starting count describes both regions together. Subtract transferred tokens to find what remains inside.

misconceptions.description: The number transferred during a round is confused with the number remaining inside.
misconceptions.response: Transferred and remaining name different groups. Track the inside count after every transfer.

scenes.title: Where does a mouthful go?
scenes.learnerAction: Draw or describe a possible route and predict where useful parts of food might enter the rest of the body.

content.body: A fictional school group in Buchanan is preparing a poster about what happens after eating rice. Before using the poster, sketch your own idea of the route. Keep your first drawing so that you can later explain a change.

prompts.prompt: What route do you predict, and where might useful parts leave it? Label one uncertainty in your first model.

scenes.title: Build a connected food route
scenes.learnerAction: Arrange the route, move the token through it and sort the organs into food-path or juice-supply groups. Never put model materials in your mouth.

content.body: Use large paper cards and a paper food token. Move the token from mouth to anus through the route you arrange. Chewing starts breakdown; the esophagus moves food; the stomach mixes it. Digestion continues in the small intestine, where most nutrients are absorbed. The large intestine absorbs water. Its rectum stores stool before it leaves through the anus. The liver and pancreas supply juices; swallowed food does not pass through them.

hints: Follow the connected tube from the mouth through the stomach and intestines.
An organ can supply a juice without being a place the swallowed food passes through.

scenes.title: Crossing a wall does not mean disappearing
scenes.learnerAction: Follow the two transfers, compare the graph with the tokens, and account for all twelve tokens in both regions.

content.body: Draw two regions: inside the small intestine, and the rest of the body. Use twelve large paper tokens for already-digested nutrients. Move five across the boundary, then five more. Keep transferred tokens in the body region. This represents absorption, not whole food leaving the stomach. The counts are invented for the model; they are not a human absorption rate.

scenes.title: Operate and check your own paper model
scenes.learnerAction: Move the nine tokens, record both counts and explain what the boundary crossing represents.

content.body: Use fourteen large paper tokens, drawn marks or counters too large to swallow. Mark an inside region and a body region. Move nine tokens across the wall. Keep every token visible. A crossing changes its region, not whether it exists. Starting, transferred and remaining counts describe different groups. Count both regions before answering. A partner may move tokens while you direct. Keep objects away from mouths.

prompts.prompt: Explain what one crossing models. Name one thing these paper tokens do not show about a real intestine.

hints: The starting count includes both regions. A transferred token is no longer inside.
A token that crosses remains visible in the body region. Add both regions to check the total.

scenes.title: Interpret a new model independently
scenes.learnerAction: Determine the tokens left inside after each round, then explain where the rest are and why the model total stays constant.

content.body: A different paper model starts with sixteen nutrient tokens inside. Five cross during the first round, then eight more cross during the second. Use a drawing or paper tokens independently. These specified movements describe a model, not observations of a real person's digestion.

prompts.prompt: Where are the tokens that crossed? Explain what the model can show about absorption and why it cannot tell you a real digestion time.

scenes.title: Separate a model from evidence about a body
scenes.learnerAction: Choose the statement that matches the model and identify a claim that would need different evidence.

content.body: Compare your first route with the organ model. Explain a change using the job of an organ. The token model helps show a transfer across a wall. It does not reproduce living tissue or measure how quickly a person's body absorbs a meal.

hints: Separate a path through an organ from a juice entering that path.
Counted paper tokens can represent a transfer but cannot measure living tissue.

scenes.title: Improve the Buchanan school group's poster
scenes.learnerAction: Write or dictate 30 to 60 words correcting both claims and explaining one limitation of your model.

content.body: The fictional poster says: Food passes through the liver before reaching the stomach. The stomach absorbs all nutrients. Use the route and transfer models to replace both claims. Explain the corrections so a younger reader could follow them, while keeping the diagram's limits clear.

prompts.prompt: Correct the two poster claims using the connected route and the job of the small intestine. State one limitation. For an advanced challenge, design a clearer model that distinguishes breaking food down from absorbing the resulting nutrients, and explain how you would check its clarity.
